title: Hunted in the hills
hookLine: Mughal armies pursue Banda through the hills for years

lines: A SIKH WEARS BANDA SINGH'S CLOTHES.
OUT INTO THE HILLS BY NIGHT.
cards: Night at Lohgarh. The fort in the hills is surrounded. The emperor's army has come north in force, and the walls won't hold much longer.
Inside, tradition says, one Sikh makes an offer. He'll put on Banda Singh's clothes and sit where Banda Singh sits, so that when the enemy breaks in, they'll think they have their man.
In the dark, the real Banda Singh slips out through the hills with whoever can follow. By morning the fort has fallen, and the man they capture isn't the one they came for.

teach.h: A LONG STRETCH WITH NO GRAND BATTLES.
teach.b: That night begins a long stretch of Banda Singh's life with no grand battles to name it. The Mughal armies kept after him, season after season, through the hills and the jungles at the edge of the plains.
He'd vanish, regroup, strike, and vanish again. Lands won were lost. Towns changed hands.
The people who sheltered his men paid a price. Sikh tellings don't make this part glamorous: cold camps, short food, running at night, the slow grind of being hunted. What kept them going?
Sikhs have a phrase for it that appears at the end of the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings: chardi kala.
It means something like rising spirits, an ever-ascending spirit. Not cheerfulness, and not pretending things are fine. Chardi kala is the steadiness to keep facing upward when every report is bad.
In the Ardas it's paired with a wish for the good of all, which says something about where that spirit is meant to point. And notice the man who wore Banda Singh's clothes.
Earlier on this path, at Chamkaur, tradition told of a Sikh named Sangat Singh who wore the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away. Now it happens again.
That pattern is its own kind of chardi kala: a willingness to stand in someone else's place so the work can keep going. The hills didn't change the hard news.
But one borrowed set of clothes bought one night, and one night was enough to keep going.

how: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's years of being pursued through the hills as a time of chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, a phrase that closes the Ardas said at Sikh gatherings.

o: rising spirits, steady when news is bad
a cheerful mood that hides real trouble
the last stand of a fort under siege

games.q: your fort is surrounded, the walls won't hold, and the army wants you above all. what do you do?
o: fight at the gate until the end.
slip out by night while a friend takes your place.
games.why: tradition says a Sikh put on Banda Singh's clothes and sat in his place, and Banda Singh escaped into the hills.

practice: Name, quietly, the thing in your week that feels like being hunted: the deadline, the bill, the worry that keeps finding you, and don't fight it.
Then find one small next step, the size of one night's walk in the hills, not the whole road, and rest your attention on that step and on your breathing.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the words chardi kala sit beside it.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala, rising spirits. The steadiness Banda Singh and his men kept through the long hunt in the hills and jungles after Lohgarh fell.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising or ever-ascending spirits.

carryVoice: Your line: keep going. One night at a time still counts as going. Day eight hundred forty-three, done.
